[p. 3]

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat Fatihat al-Kitab (The Opening of the Book)

Fatihat al-shay' (the opening of a thing) is its beginning and its start. When the Noble Revelation was opened with it, either by revelation (tawqif) from the Prophet ﷺ or by the personal reasoning (ijtihad) of the Companions, as al-Qadi al-Baqillani related the two opinions concerning the order of the Revelation, it was named accordingly.

Al-Sayyid al-Jurjani said: "Fatihat al-Kitab became a proper name by predominance for the Surah of Praise (surat al-Hamd). It may also be called simply 'al-Fatiha' (the Opener). Either this is another proper name, also by predominance, since the definite article (al-) is then obligatory; or it is an abbreviation, with the article serving as a substitute for the genitive construction 'of the Book', while the original descriptive sense is still implied."

Ibn Jarir said: "It was called 'Fatihat al-Kitab' because the mushafs begin with writing it, and it is recited at the beginning of the prayers. Thus it is the opening (fawatih) of what follows it of the Surahs of the Qur'an, in writing and in recitation."

It is also called "Umm al-Qur'an" (the Mother of the Qur'an), because it precedes all other Surahs of the Qur'an, while everything else comes after it in recitation and writing; the mother and the origin are placed first. Or it is so named because it contains praise of God as He deserves, worship through His commands and prohibitions, and the explanation of His promise and threat. Or it is named for the totality of its meanings: theoretical wisdom, practical rulings, which are following the Straight Path, and awareness of the ascent-routes of the blessed and the abodes of the wretched.

The Arabs call every comprehensive matter "umm" (a mother), and every leader to which subsidiary matters attach is called "umm". Thus they call the membrane that encloses the brain "umm al-ra's" (the mother of the head), and they call the army's banner under which they gather "umm".

It is also called "al-Sab' al-Mathani" (the seven oft-repeated). Mathani is either the plural of mathna, on the pattern of mafal as a noun of place, or it is muthanna, with doubled consonant, from the verb of repetition (tathniya), in an irregular formation. It is so named because it consists of seven verses that are repeated (tuthanna) in the prayer, that is, recited again within it.

The majority of scholars hold that al-Fatiha is Meccan and that it has seven verses.

The original linguistic meaning of "surah" is a station among the stations of elevation. From this comes "sur" (wall) of a city, for the wall that encloses it, because of its height above what it encloses. From this is the saying of Nabigha of Banu Dhubyan:

"Have you not seen that God has given you a surah (a rank),
Above which every king wavers?"

That is, a station of honour, which the stations of kings fall short of.

As for "ayah", it means either "sign" (al-'alama), because it is a sign by which the completion of what precedes it and the beginning of what follows it are known, like a sign that indicates a thing and is used as evidence for it; or it means "story" (al-qissa), as Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said:

"Now convey this message (ayah) to al-Mu'arrid,
Is he awake when he speaks the word, or is he dreaming?"

That is, a message from me and a report about me. Thus the meaning of "ayat" is "stories", one story following another.

On the interpretation of His Exalted saying:

[1] ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾

Imam Ibn Jarir said: "God, may His remembrance be exalted and His names be sanctified, taught His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ good manners by instructing him to mention His Beautiful Names before all his actions, and He prescribed for him to describe Him with them before all his important affairs. He made what He taught him of this a path for all His creatures: a sunnah they follow and a way they walk upon. Thus with it they begin the openings of their speech, the headings of their letters and books, and their needs. So much so that the indication of what is manifest in the words of the speaker, 'In the name of God', suffices as an indication of what is hidden of his intent, which is omitted. For the preposition 'bi' (in) requires a verb that it governs; when that verb is omitted, it is to be supplied as that by which the naming becomes the starting point. Here 'ism' (name) means 'tasmiya' (naming), like 'kalam' (speech) means 'takllim' (speaking), and 'ata' (gift) means 'i'ta' (giving). The meaning is: I read by the naming of God and His mention, and I begin the recitation by naming God with His Beautiful Names and His Exalted Attributes. 'Allah' is a proper name for His essence, exalted and sanctified. Ibn 'Abbas said: He is the One whom everything worships (ya'lahuhu) and serves. Its origin is 'Ilah' in the sense of 'ma'luh' (one who is worshipped), meaning worshipped. When the definite article (al-) was added to it, the hamza was dropped for lightness, because it is very frequent in speech. After the assimilation, it was pronounced with emphasis (fukhkhima) as a sign of glorification. This is the verification of the linguists."

On "al-Rahman al-Rahim", al-Jawhari said: "They are two names derived from mercy (al-rahma). Their parallel in the language is 'nadim' and 'nadman' (companion), and both have the same meaning. It is permissible to repeat two names when their derivations differ, for emphasis, as one says 'jadd mujidd' (earnest and striving). However, 'al-Rahman' is a name specific to God, and it is not permissible for anyone else to be named by it. Do you not see that He said: ﴿Say: Call upon God or call upon the Most Gracious﴾ [al-Isra' 110], thus He placed beside it the name in which none shares with Him?" End of quotation.

Al-Allama al-Shaykh Muhammad 'Abduh al-Misri disputed, in some of his exegetical discussions, the view that "al-Rahman al-Rahim" have one meaning. He said: "That is an oversight, and we ask God to pardon its holder." Then he said: "I do not permit any Muslim to say, in himself or with his tongue, that there is in the Qur'an a word that came to emphasize another and has no meaning of its own. Rather, there is in the Qur'an no particle that came without an intended meaning. The majority hold that the meaning of 'al-Rahman' is the Bestower of great blessings, and the meaning of 'al-Rahim' is the Bestower of subtle blessings. Some say: 'al-Rahman' is the Bestower of general blessings that include disbelievers along with others, and 'al-Rahim' is the Bestower of special blessings for the believers. All of this is an arbitrary judgement about the language, based on the assumption that increase in the form indicates increase in meaning. But increase only indicates the attribute in general. So the form 'al-Rahman' indicates abundance of the beneficence He gives, whether it is great (jalil) or subtle (daqiq). As for the claim that the individual instances of beneficence indicated by the longer word are greater in number than the individual instances indicated by the shorter word, that is neither intended nor meant. Whoever said that the meaning of 'al-Rahman' is the one who does general beneficence came close, but he erred in restricting the signification of 'al-Rahim' to the believers. Perhaps what led those who said that the second is emphatic of the first to this view is their failure to be persuaded by what they stated regarding the distinction, together with their failure to perceive what is better than it." Then he said: "What I say is: the word 'Rahman' is a verbal attribute with the sense of intensity, like 'fa'alan', and in the usage of the language it indicates temporary attributes, like 'atshan' (thirsty), 'ghirthan' (hungry), and 'ghadban' (angry). As for the word 'Rahim', in usage it indicates enduring meanings, such as character traits and dispositions in people, like 'alim' (knowing), 'hakim' (wise), 'halim' (forbearing), and 'jamil' (beautiful). The Qur'an does not depart from the eloquent Arabic style in describing the attributes of God, Mighty and Majestic, which are exalted above resemblance to the attributes of creatures. Thus the word 'al-Rahman' indicates the One from whom the effects of mercy proceed in action, which is the outpouring of blessings and beneficence. The word 'al-Rahim' indicates the source of this mercy and beneficence, and that it is among the enduring and necessary attributes. In this sense, neither of the two attributes can dispense with the other, and the second is not emphatic of the first. When the Arab hears the description of God, may His praise be exalted, as 'al-Rahman', and understands from it that He is the one who actually bestows blessings, he does not conclude that mercy is one of the attributes necessarily belonging to Him always, because an action may cease if it is temporary and did not arise from a necessary and enduring attribute. So when he hears the word 'al-Rahim', his belief is completed in the manner that befits God Exalted and pleases Him, glory be to Him." End.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 1, verse 2:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[2] ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾

"Al-hamdu lillah" (all praise is for Allah), i.e., commendation for beauty and ascription of perfection, is established for Allah alone, apart from all that is worshipped besides Him, and apart from everything He has created. The "al-" in "al-hamd" is for comprehensiveness (istighraq), i.e., the comprehensiveness of all kinds of praise and their being established for Allah, exalted is He, as an act of glorification and exaltation, as in the hadith: "O Allah, to You belongs all praise, all of it, and to You belongs all dominion, all of it."

(p-7) The Imam Ibn al-Qayyim said in "Tariq al-Hijratayn": Dominion and praise, with respect to Him, exalted is He, are mutually entailing. Thus everything encompassed by His dominion and power is encompassed by His praise; He is praised in His dominion, and to Him belong dominion and power together with His praise. Just as it is impossible for anything among the existing things to fall outside His dominion and power, it is impossible for them to fall outside His praise and wisdom. For this reason He, glorified is He, praises Himself at the time of His creating and commanding, to alert His servants that the source of His creating and commanding is His praiseworthiness. He is praised for all that He created and commanded, as the praise of thankfulness and worship, and the praise of commendation and eulogy. Both are united by "tabaraka" (blessed is), and "Tabaraka Allah" (Blessed is Allah) encompasses all of that. For this reason He mentioned this word after His saying: ﴿Surely, His is the creation and the command. Blessed is Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-A'raf: 54]. Thus "al-hamd" is the broadest of attributes and the most general of eulogies. The paths to knowledge of it are extremely numerous, and the ways to contemplate it in the atoms of the world and its particulars, and in the details of command and prohibition, are very vast, because all His names, blessed and exalted is He, are praiseworthy; His attributes are praiseworthy; His acts are praiseworthy; His rulings are praiseworthy; His justice is praiseworthy; His retribution against His enemies is praiseworthy; and His bounty in His kindness to His friends is praiseworthy. Creation and command arose only through His praise, came into being through His praise, and manifested through His praise, and the ultimate end is His praise. So His praise is the cause of that, its end, its manifestation and its bearer. His praise is the spirit of everything, the subsistence of everything is through His praise, the pervasion of His praise in existing things and the appearance of its traces in them is a matter witnessed by the eyes and the insights. [Ibn al-Qayyim] then said: In sum, every attribute of loftiness, every beautiful name, every fine praise, and every praise, glorification, declaration of transcendence, sanctification, majesty and honour is for Allah, mighty and majestic, in the most perfect, complete and enduring manner; and all that He is described by, mentioned by, and reported of by is a praise of Him, a commendation, a glorification and a sanctification. So, Glorified is He and praised, no one of His creation can enumerate praise of Him. End of quote.

"Rabb al-'alamin" (Lord of the worlds): "al-Rabb" is applied to the master who is obeyed, to the reformer, and to the owner. You say: "rabbahu yarubbuhu, fa-huwa rabb," as you say: "namma 'alayhi yannimmu, fa-huwa namm." So it is an attributive adjective (sifah mushabbahah). It may also be a verbal noun (masdar) in the sense of "tarbiyah" (nurturing), which is bringing a thing to its perfection gradually, and the agent is described by it as an intensive form, just as He is described as "al-'adl" (the just). "Al-Rabb," with the definite article, is said only of Allah, mighty and majestic. In other than Him it is restricted by an idafah (annexation), as in "rabb al-dar" (master of the house), and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Return to your lord﴾ [Yusuf: 50], ﴿Surely he is my lord; he has made my abode goodly﴾ [Yusuf: 23].

"Al-'alamin" is the plural of "'alam," which means all creation and every kind within it. The choice of the plural form serves to show the comprehensiveness of His lordship, exalted is He, over all kinds, and the definite article is for the comprehensiveness of each of their individuals, all of them.

The commentary on the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[3] ﴿The Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾

Their mention together establishes the attribute of lordship (rubbubiyyah) by way of pairing encouragement with warning (tarhib), which is the method of the wise Revelation.

The Discourse on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:

[4] ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾

ʿĀṣim and al-Kisāʾī read "Māliki" with an alif (ʾalif), while the rest read it without the alif. Al-Zamakhsharī said: The reading "Maliki" (King of the Day of Judgment) has been preferred, because it is the reading of the people of the two Sanctuaries (Mecca and Medina), who are the most worthy of people to recite the Qur'an fresh and tender as it was revealed, and their reciters are the most eminent in transmission and eloquence. Also, due to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whose is the dominion today?﴾ [Ghafir: 16], so He has described His essence as the King on the Day of Resurrection. The Qur'an supports one part of it with another, and its meanings are harmonious in their subject matters. There are other preferences as well.

Some have said: The reading "Māliki" is more eloquent, because the king (malik) is the one who manages the general affairs of his subjects, and has no authority over their particular matters. The distinction becomes apparent in the case of a enslaved servant within a kingdom that has a sultan: there is no doubt that his owner (mālik) is the one who takes charge of all his affairs, not the sultan. Among the aspects of its preference: it has one letter more, and for the reciter of the Qur'an there are ten good deeds for every letter, as related by al-Tirmidhī from Ibn Masʿūd with a sound chain of narration. Both readings are sound and mutawatir (widely transmitted) among the Seven Readings.

And "al-Dīn" means the reckoning and the recompense for deeds. From it comes the saying: "As you judge, so you will be judged." That is: the Master of all the affairs of all worlds on the Day of Judgment. Its being specified by the genitive construction is either to magnify and inspire awe of Him, or to show that He alone executes the matter and decides the judgment therein.

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

﴿Thee alone do we worship, and Thee alone do we ask for help.﴾

al-Tabari said: That is, to You, O God, we submit, we humble ourselves, and we abase ourselves, acknowledging Your lordship and not that of anyone else. He said: Among all the Arabs, *ʿubūdiyyah* (servitude, worship) is rooted in humbling oneself. They call a road that has been made smooth, which feet have trodden and travellers have levelled, *muʿabbad* (paved). From this root the camel that has been tamed through riding for errands is called *muʿabbad*, and from it the slave is called *ʿabd* ("slave") because of his submission to his master. End of quote.

In this verse is an announcement of what Islam proclaimed: the liberation of souls for God, Exalted is He, and their dedication to worshipping Him alone. That is, one must not associate anything with Him: not in love comparable to His love, nor in fear, nor in hope, [p-10] nor in reliance upon Him, nor in action done for Him, nor in vows made to Him, nor in submission to Him, nor in abasement, veneration, prostration, or seeking nearness. All of this is due only to the Originator of the heavens and the earth, alone. The word *ʿibādah* (worship) comprises the perfection of humility together with the perfection of love. The worshipper must therefore love the worshipped God with perfect love, and must be humbled before Him with perfect humility. Neither of these is suitable except for God alone. He is the God who deserves worship, and none deserves it but Him. Worship consists of perfect love, humility, reverence, reliance, and supplication for what none but Him can grant, exalted is He. The fronting of the object (*taqdīm al-mafʿūl*, placing "Thee" before the verb) points to this, for in it is an alert to what is obligatory for the servant: that he single out his Lord for worship and submit his face to God alone. This is unlike the condition of the polytheists whom the Prophet ﷺ overcame. They were scattered in their worship and divided in their direction. Among them were those who worshipped the sun and the moon, those who worshipped the angels, those who worshipped idols, those who worshipped rabbis and monks, and those who worshipped trees and stones, and so on, as the Noble Qur'an explains in His words: ﴿And among His signs are the night and the day, and the sun and the moon. Do not prostrate to the sun or to the moon﴾ [Fussilat: 37], and so on. In His words: ﴿And on the Day He will gather them all, and say to the angels, "Did these worship you?"﴾ [Saba': 40] ﴿They will say, "Glory be to You! You are our Guardian, not them. Rather, they used to worship the jinn; most of them were believers in them."﴾ [Saba': 41]. In His words: ﴿And when God said, "O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as two gods besides God?'" He said, "Glory be to You…"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116], and so on. And His words: ﴿Nor would He command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords﴾ [Al 'Imran: 80], and so on. In His words: ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza?﴾ [al-Najm: 19] ﴿and Manat, the third, the other?﴾ [al-Najm: 20]. And the hadith of Abu Waqid al-Laythi, who said: "We went out with the Messenger of God ﷺ to Hunayn, and we were recently converted from disbelief. The polytheists had a lote tree where they would sit in devotion and hang their weapons, called *Dhat Anwat*. We passed by a lote tree and said, 'O Messenger of God, make for us a *Dhat Anwat* as they have a *Dhat Anwat*.' The Messenger of God ﷺ said, 'God is greatest! This is the way of the ancients. By Him in whose hand my soul is, you have said what the Children of Israel said to Moses: ﴿Make for us a god as they have gods." He said, "Surely you are a people who are ignorant.﴾ [al-A'raf: 138] up to His words: ﴿and that He preferred you above the worlds﴾ [al-A'raf: 140].'" Related by al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sound.

As for their worship of rabbis and monks, it is in His words: ﴿They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides God﴾ [al-Tawbah: 31]. Imam Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi related from 'Adi ibn Hatim that he heard the Prophet ﷺ recite this verse: ﴿They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides God﴾ [al-Tawbah: 31], and so on. He said: "I said to him, 'We do not worship them.' He said, 'Do they not forbid what God has permitted, so you forbid it, and make lawful what God has forbidden, so you make it lawful?' I said, 'Yes.' He said, 'That is their worship.'"

Thus worship has kinds and categories, and faith is not complete except by affirming the oneness of all of them for God, glorified is He. The Sunnah has explained that supplication is worship, that is, its essential and greatest pillar. Its source in the Noble Revelation is His words: ﴿Your Lord said, "Call upon Me, and I will respond to you. Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me…"﴾ [Ghafir: 60]. So he named it worship.

[p-13] And in a report: "Association in this nation is more hidden than the crawling of an ant."

Shams al-Din ibn al-Qayyim said: For this reason the servant is commanded in every prayer to say, "Thee alone do we worship, and Thee alone do we ask for help." Satan commands association, and the soul obeys him in this, so the soul continues to turn toward other than God, either out of fear of Him or hope in Him. The servant therefore always needs to purify his monotheism from the taints of association. For this reason He, glorified is He, informed us that the polytheists did not measure Him with His due measure in three places of His Book. How can one measure Him with His due measure when he has made for Him equals and rivals, loving them, fearing them, hoping in them, humbling himself and submitting to them, fleeing from their displeasure, and preferring their pleasure? The one who is preferred does not accept being preferred over Him. End of quote.

(Benefit) Some of the early generations (*al-salaf*, the pious predecessors) said: The Fatihah is the secret of the Qur'an, and its secret is this statement, "Thee alone do we worship, and Thee alone do we ask for help." The first part is a disavowal of association, and the second is a disavowal of one's own power and strength, and a committing of affairs to God, mighty and majestic is He. This meaning appears in more than one verse of the Qur'an, as He said: ﴿So worship Him and rely upon Him﴾ [Hud: 123]. ﴿Say, "He is the Most Merciful. We have believed in Him and upon Him we rely."﴾ [al-Mulk: 29]. ﴿Lord of the East and the West; there is no god but He, so take Him as a guardian﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 9].

(p-14) The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:
[6] ﴿Guide us to the straight path.﴾
That is: inspire us with the guiding way, direct us to it, and grant us success in it.

Imam al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said in his tafsir: "Guidance (al-hidayah) is gentle indication (dalalah bi-lutf), and from it comes al-hadiyyah (the gift), and hawadi al-wahsh (the forerunners of the wild animals), which are their vanguard, since they lead the rest. He restricted what is indication to the form fa'ala, as in hadaytuhu al-tariq (I showed him the way), and what is giving to the form af'ala, as in ahdaytu al-hadiyyah (I presented the gift). And for the bride who is displayed (tusawwiru al-'arus) there are two forms, and it is said: hadaytu and ahdaytu. If it is asked: how do you make guidance an indication of gentleness, when He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So guide them to the path of Hellfire﴾ [al-Saffat: 23], and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is decreed for him that whoever takes him as an ally, he will misguide him and guide him to the punishment of the Blaze﴾ [al-Hajj: 4]? It is said: this is according to their usage of the word in mockery, as the poet said:
"And cavalry that I have advanced upon with cavalry — their greeting among them is a painful blow!"
Guidance is the direction toward good things, in word and deed, and it comes from Allah, exalted is He, in stages, some of which follow from others: the second cannot occur except after the first, nor the third except after the second. The first stage is His giving the servant the faculties by which he is guided to his interests, either by subjugation or by choice, such as the five senses and the faculty of thought. Some of this He gave to animals, and some He reserved for humans. This is indicated by His words: ﴿Who gave everything its creation, then guided [it]﴾ [Ta-Ha: 50], and His words: ﴿And the One who measured, then guided﴾ [al-A'la: 3]. This guidance is either subjugation or teaching, and to this type He alluded in His words: ﴿And your Lord inspired the bee﴾ [al-Nahl: 68], and His words: ﴿Because your Lord inspired it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 5]. And He said regarding man, in respect of the intellect He gave him and the right judgment He made him know: ﴿Indeed, We guided him to the way﴾ [al-Insan: 3], and He said: ﴿And We guided him to the two highways﴾ [al-Balad: 10], and He said concerning Thamud: ﴿And We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fussilat: 17].

The second is guidance through invocation (al-du'a') and the sending of the prophets, peace be upon them. It is this that He meant by His words: ﴿And We made from among them leaders guiding by Our command﴾ [al-Sajdah: 24], and by His words: ﴿And for every people there is a guide﴾ [al-Ra'd: 7]. This guidance is attributed sometimes to Allah, exalted is He, sometimes to the Prophet, peace be upon him, and sometimes to the Qur'an. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾ [al-Isra': 9].

The third is guidance that the righteous of His servants attain through the good they have earned, and this is the guidance mentioned in His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And they were guided to good speech, and were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy﴾ [al-Hajj: 24], and His words: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 90], and His words: ﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our ways﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 69]. This guidance is what is meant by His words: ﴿And He will make for you a light by which you will walk﴾ [al-Hadid: 28].

It is correct to attribute this guidance to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, so it is said: He bestowed it upon them insofar as He is the cause of their reaching it. And it is correct to say: they earned it insofar as they reached it through their own striving. Thus, if someone seeks a sultan for support and he gives him, it is correct to say: the sultan bestowed on him; and it is correct to say: so-and-so earned it by his effort. Because this encompasses both matters, Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance and gives them their piety﴾ [Muhammad: 17], and He said: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, their Lord will guide them by their faith﴾ [Yunus: 9]. Thus He indicated that this is by their effort and by His grace together.

This guidance may be said to be permitted to all intelligent beings, and it may be said to be restricted (p-17) except to His allies, since it is possible for all intelligent beings to prepare themselves to receive it. For this reason it is said: it is not easy to receive it before a person takes on a particular form through the performance of acts of worship. Some verifiers have said: the guidance from Allah is abundant, but only the discerning perceives it, and only a few act upon it. Do you not see that the stars of the sky are so many, yet only the scholars are guided by them? Some of the friends of Allah said: the likeness of Allah's guidance among people is like a torrent that passes over hollows and pools, so each hollow takes according to its capacity. Then he recited His words: ﴿He sends down water from the sky, and valleys flow according to their measure﴾ [al-Ra'd: 17]. Others said: it is like rain that falls upon lands, and each land benefits according to its readiness to benefit from it.

(The fourth stage): of guidance is the enabling of entry into the neighborhood of Him in the abode of eternity. It is this that Allah meant by His words: ﴿And We will remove whatever ill feeling is in their breasts; rivers will flow beneath them, and they will say: Praise be to Allah who guided us to this﴾ [al-A'raf: 43]. Once this is established, some guidance cannot be denied of anyone in any respect, and some of it is denied of some and affirmed for others. In this respect, Allah, exalted is He, said to His Prophet ﷺ: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ [al-Qasas: 56], and He said: ﴿Their guidance is not incumbent upon you, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah: 272], and He said: ﴿Nor are you a guide for the blind away from their error﴾ [al-Naml: 81]. Here He meant the guidance which is divine success and entry into Paradise, not the guidance which is invocation, as shown by His words: ﴿And indeed, you guide to a straight path﴾ [al-Shura: 52], and He said concerning the prophets: ﴿And We made them leaders guiding by Our command﴾ [al-Anbiya': 73].

So His words: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ have been explained in several ways according to differing viewpoints on the aspects of guidance mentioned above:

(First): that it means general guidance, and He commanded us to ask for it, though He has certainly already granted it, so that He may increase us in reward for the supplication, just as He commanded us to say: "O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad."
(Second): it was said: grant us success in the way of the Law (shar').
(Third): protect us from being led astray by the misguided and from being enticed by desires, and keep us safe from doubts.
(Fourth): increase us in guidance, seeking success in what You promised by Your words: ﴿And whoever believes in Allah, He will guide his heart﴾ [al-Taghabun: 11], and Your words: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance﴾ [Muhammad: 17].
(Fifth): it was said: teach us the true knowledge, for that is the cause of deliverance, which is what is expressed as light in His words: ﴿Allah guides to His light whom He wills﴾ [al-Nur: 35].
(Sixth): it was said: it is the request for Paradise, due to His words: ﴿And those who are killed in the cause of Allah, He will not let their deeds be lost﴾ [Muhammad: 4], ﴿He will guide them and set right their affairs﴾ [Muhammad: 5], and He said: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, their Lord will guide them by their faith﴾ [Yunus: 9], etc.

These sayings differ according to the differences in their viewpoints regarding parts and particulars of guidance, and all of them may be intended by the verse, since there is no contradiction among them. (p-20) And success is with Allah." End of al-Raghib's words. By this the true meaning of guidance in all its occurrences in the Noble Revelation becomes known, and that the reported interpretations of a verse, when they do not contradict one another, may all be intended. Such a thing is called difference of variety (ikhtilaf tanawwu'), not difference of contradiction (ikhtilaf tadad).

As Shaykh al-Islam Taqi al-Din Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, indicated in an important discussion of his, which we quote here for its great benefits, he said, may Allah have mercy on him:

It should be known that the disagreement that occurs among commentators and others is of two kinds:

The first contains no opposition or contradiction; rather, each of the two views may be true. It is only a difference of variety, or a difference in attributes or expressions. The general disagreement reported from the commentators among the Companions and the Followers is of this kind. When Allah, glorified is He, mentions a name in the Qur'an, such as His words "Guide us to the straight path," every commentator expresses the straight path with a phrase that indicates some of its attributes, and all of these are true, just as Allah, His Messenger, and His Book are named by names, each of which indicates an attribute of His. Some say: the straight path is the Book of Allah, or following the Book of Allah. Another says: the straight path is Islam, or the religion of Islam. Another says: the straight path is the Sunnah and the Community. Another says: the straight path is the way of servitude, or the way of fear, hope, and love, and carrying out what is commanded and avoiding what is forbidden, or following the Book and the Sunnah, or acting in obedience to Allah, or similar names and expressions. It is known that the named reality is one, even though its attributes vary and its names and expressions are multiplied. Much of the tafsir and translation is of this kind.

Another kind is that the commentator or translator mentions the meaning of a term by way of example, not as a definition or exhaustive limit. For instance, if a non-Arab asks: what is the meaning of "bread?" he is pointed to a loaf, not that the intended thing is merely that particular object, but the pointing is to specify this individual as an example. This is like when they are asked about His words: ﴿Then among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one foremost in good deeds﴾ [Fatir: 32] (p-21), or about His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him and those who are doers of good﴾ [al-Nahl: 128], or about the righteous or the wrongdoers, and similar general comprehensive names whose full meaning may be difficult or impossible for the listener or speaker to fully grasp. Since he does not need all of it, he mentions to him some of its types and individuals by which his purpose is achieved, and he may use it to infer its counterparts. The one who wrongs himself is the one who leaves what is commanded and does what is forbidden; the moderate one does what is obligatory and leaves what is unlawful; the foremost in good deeds does what is obligatory and recommended and leaves what is unlawful and disliked. So the answerer, according to the questioner's need, says: the wrongdoer is the one who misses the prayer, or who does not complete the ablution, or who does not perfect the pillars, and similar things. The moderate one is the one who prays on time as he is commanded, and the foremost in good deeds is the one who prays with its obligations and recommended acts and adds the voluntary prayers along with it. Likewise one says the same in regard to zakah, fasting, hajj, and all the other obligations.

It has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: Tafsir is of four kinds: a tafsir known to the Arabs from their speech; a tafsir whose ignorance no one is excused for; a tafsir known to the scholars; and a tafsir known only to Allah. Whoever claims knowledge of the last is a liar.

The Companions took from the Messenger the wording of the Qur'an and its meaning, just as they took the Sunnah from him. And although some people altered the Sunnah, some people altered some meanings of the Qur'an, since they could not change its wording. Also, some meanings of the Qur'an may be hidden from some scholars, just as some of the Sunnah was hidden from them, so the errors of the mujtahids occur in this domain, and Allah knows best.

An extended discussion of this topic was given in the introduction of this book, so refer back to it. (See: vol. 1, p. 17).

(p-22) Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, also said, in verifying this verse:

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 1, verse 6 (part 2 of 2):**

Every servant is constantly in need of the object of this supplication, which is guidance to the Straight Path (al-sirat al-mustaqim), for there is no deliverance from punishment except through this guidance, and no arrival at happiness except by it. Whoever misses this guidance is either among "those who have earned anger" (al-maghdub 'alayhim) or among "those who are astray" (al-dallin). This guidance is attained only through the guidance of God: ﴿Whomever God guides is the one truly guided, but whomever He leaves astray, you will not find for him any protecting friend to guide him﴾ [al-Kahf: 17]. The Straight Path is that you do, at every time, what you have been commanded to do at that time, in knowledge and action, and that you do not do what you have been forbidden. This requires, at every time, that you know what He has commanded at that time and what He has forbidden, and that there arise in you a firm resolve to do what is commanded and a aversion to abandoning what is prohibited.

The Straight Path has been explained as the Qur'an, as Islam, and as the paths of worship ('ubudiyyah), and all of this is true; it is described by all of these and by other things. Therefore, his need for this guidance is essential for his happiness and deliverance. This is unlike the need for provision (rizq) and victory (nasr), for God provides for him, and if his provision is cut off he dies, and death is unavoidable. If he is among the people of guidance, he will be happy after death, and death will be the means of bringing him to lasting, everlasting happiness, so it becomes a mercy for him. Likewise victory: if it is decreed that he is overcome and defeated until he is killed, then if he is among those guided to steadfastness, he dies as a martyr (shahid), and being killed is part of the completion of God's blessing upon him. Thus it becomes clear that the servants' need for guidance is greater than their need for provision and victory; rather, there is no comparison between them. For this reason this supplication was made obligatory upon them in the prayers, both the obligatory and the voluntary.

Also, this supplication includes provision and victory, because when one is guided to the Straight Path, he is among the God-fearing: ﴿And whoever fears God, He will make for him a way out﴾ [al-Talaq: 2], ﴿and will provide for him from where he does not expect﴾ [al-Talaq: 3], and he is among those who rely upon God: ﴿And whoever relies upon God, then He is sufficient for him. Indeed, God will accomplish His purpose﴾ [al-Talaq: 3], and he is among those whom God and His Messenger support, and whoever supports God, God will support him, and he is among the soldiers of God, and the soldiers of God are the victorious. So complete guidance includes the attainment of the greatest of what brings provision and victory. Thus it becomes clear that this supplication is the comprehensive one for every desired thing through which every benefit is attained and every harm is averted.

(Benefit): The Straight Path originally means the clear road that has no crookedness or deviation in it, and it is used figuratively for every saying or action by which its doer reaches the praiseworthy goal. The clear road for the senses is like the truth for the intellect, in that when one travels by them both, they bring the traveler to the best outcome.

**The interpretation of His saying (Exalted is He):**
[7] ﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray.﴾

That is, by Your obedience and Your worship. They are the ones mentioned in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger – those are with the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favour of the prophets, the steadfast in truth (ṣiddīqīn), the martyrs, and the righteous.﴾ [al-Nisa': 69]

(p-24) "Not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray." Al-Iṣfahānī said: Exalted is He mentioned this phrase because the disbelievers had shared with the believers in many of the bounties bestowed on them. So He clarified by this description that what is meant by the supplication is not the general bounties, but that it is a special bounty. Then, what is meant by "those who have earned anger" and "those who are astray" is every person who has deviated from the highway of Islam, from whatever sect or creed. Some exegetes specifying one particular group among them is by way of giving an example of the general through its clearest and most well-known instances. This is what is meant by the statement of Ibn Abī Ḥātim: "I know of no disagreement among the exegetes that those who have earned anger are the Jews, and those who are astray are the Christians."

**Benefits (Fawā'id):**

**The first:** It is recommended for one who recites al-Fātiḥah to say after it: "Āmīn." Its meaning is: "O Allah, answer," or "So let it be," or "So do [it]." It is not part of the Qur'an, as evidenced by the fact that it is not established in the codices (maṣāḥif). The evidence for the recommendation of saying āmīn is what Imam Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd, and al-Tirmidhī narrated from Wā'il ibn Ḥujr, who said: "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) recite ﴿not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray﴾, and he said: 'Āmīn,' prolonging his voice with it." In Abū Dāwūd's version: "He raised his voice with it." Al-Tirmidhī said: "This is a ḥasan hadith (sound-good). On the subject there are also reports from 'Alī and Abū Hurayrah, and it is narrated from 'Alī, Ibn Mas'ūd, and others."

And from Abū Hurayrah, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited ﴿not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray﴾, he would say: 'Āmīn,' until those who were next to him in the first row could hear it." Narrated by Abū Dāwūd.

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs (Bukhārī and Muslim), from Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the imam says āmīn, then say āmīn, for whoever's āmīn coincides with the āmīn of the angels, Allah will forgive him his previous sins."

In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abū Mūsā, raised (to the Prophet): "When he (i.e., the imam) says: ﴿nor of those who are astray﴾, then say: 'Āmīn,' and Allah will answer you."

**The second:** Concerning mention of the sciences contained in this sūrah.

Know that this noble sūrah – and it is seven verses – includes praise of Allah (Exalted is He), glorifying Him and extolling Him by mentioning His Most Beautiful Names, which necessitate His Sublime Attributes; it includes mention of the Return (al-Ma'ād), which is the Day of Judgement (Yawm al-Dīn); and it guides His servants to ask Him, to supplicate humbly to Him, and to disavow their own power and strength; and to sincerely devote worship to Him, affirming His unity in divinity (tawḥīd al-ulūhiyyah), blessed and exalted is He, and declaring Him free from having any partner, equal, or like; and it includes their request that He guide them to the straight path – which is the upright religion – and that He make them steadfast upon it, until it leads them to the gardens of bliss, in the company of the prophets, the ṣiddīqīn, the martyrs, and the righteous.

It also includes encouragement toward righteous deeds so that they may be with their people on the Day of Resurrection, and warning against the ways of falsehood lest they be gathered with its travelers on the Day of Resurrection – and those are "those who have earned anger" and "those who are astray."

Allamah Shaykh Muḥammad 'Abduh said in his tafsīr:

al-Fātiḥah contains a summary of what is in the Qur'an, and everything in it is an elaboration of the principles upon which it is founded. I do not mean by this what they express by allusion and the indication of letters, such as their saying: "The secrets of the Qur'an are in al-Fātiḥah, the secrets of al-Fātiḥah are in the basmalah, the secrets of the basmalah are in the bā', and the secrets of the bā' are in its dot!" For this has not been established from the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions, may the pleasure of Allah be upon them, nor is it rational in itself; rather, it is one of the inventions of the extremists whose excess led them to nullify the Qur'an's very essence, which is clarity (al-bayān). He said: The clarification of what I intend is that the Qur'an was revealed for several purposes:

The first of them is tawḥīd (affirmation of Allah's oneness), because all people were idolaters – even if some of them claimed tawḥīd.

The second: the promise to whoever adheres to it and the giving of good tidings of a good reward, and the warning to whoever does not adhere to it and the notice of evil punishment. The promise includes what is for the community and what is for individuals, encompassing the bounties of this world and the Hereafter and their felicity. The warning likewise includes their vengeance and misery. Allah promised the believers: succession in the earth, honour, authority, and sovereignty. And He threatened those who opposed: with disgrace and misery in this world. Just as He promised in the Hereafter the Garden and bliss, and threatened the blazing Fire.

The third: worship that revives tawḥīd in hearts and firmly establishes it in souls.

The fourth: the explanation of the path of felicity and how to walk upon it, which leads to the bounties of this world and the next.

The fifth: the narratives of those who stopped at the limits of Allah (Exalted is He) and adhered to the rulings of His religion, and the reports of those who transgressed His limits and cast aside the rulings of His religion behind their backs, for the sake of taking lessons and choosing the way of the good-doers.

These are the matters which the Qur'an contains, and in them is the life of people and their worldly and otherworldly felicity; and al-Fātiḥah contains them in summary without any doubt or uncertainty.

As for tawḥīd, it is in His saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fātiḥah: 2], for it expresses that every praise and commendation arising from any blessing belongs to Him (Exalted is He). This is not valid unless He (Glorified is He) is the source of every blessing in the universe that merits praise; and among them is the blessing of creation, origination, nurturing, and development. He did not suffice with the expression's implication of this meaning, but stated it explicitly with His saying: "Lord of the worlds." The word "Rabb" does not mean merely "owner" and "master," but contains the meaning of nurturing and growth. It is explicit that every blessing a person sees in himself and in the horizons comes from Him, Mighty and Majestic. There is no one in the universe who disposes of creation, misery, and happiness besides Him. Furthermore, tawḥīd is the most important thing for which religion came. Therefore, in al-Fātiḥah He did not suffice with a mere allusion to it, but completed it with His saying: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ [al-Fātiḥah: 5], thereby uprooting the roots of association (shirk) and idolatry which were widespread among all nations: taking intermediaries apart from Allah, to whom they attribute a hidden authority, who are called upon apart from Allah, sought for help in fulfilling needs in this world, and through whom one seeks nearness to Allah. All the verses of tawḥīd in the Qur'an and its confrontation with the polytheists are an elaboration of this summary.

"As for promise and warning: the first of them is folded into ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾. The mention of mercy at the beginning of the Book is that which encompasses everything – a promise of goodness – especially since He repeated it a second time, alerting us that His command to us to affirm His oneness and worship Him is a mercy from Him (Glorified is He) toward us, because it is for our benefit and our advantage. His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿Master of the Day of Judgement﴾ [al-Fātiḥah: 4] includes both promise and warning together, because the meaning of dīn is submission. That is: for Him (Exalted is He) on that day is absolute authority and a sovereignty about which there is no dispute, neither in reality nor in claim; and the whole world will be subservient to His greatness, outwardly and inwardly, hoping for His mercy and fearing His punishment. This includes promise and warning. Or the meaning of dīn is recompense, which is either a reward for the good-doer or a punishment for the wrongdoer, and that is promise and warning. Add to that that He mentioned after it "the straight path," which whoever follows succeeds and whoever deviates from it perishes, and this necessitates promise and warning.

"As for worship: after it was mentioned in the context of tawḥīd with His saying: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ [al-Fātiḥah: 5], He clarified its meaning to some extent with His saying: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fātiḥah: 6], that is: He has set for us a path which He will make clear and define. The criterion of felicity lies in steadfastness upon it, and misery in deviating from it. This steadfastness upon it is the very spirit of worship. A similar example is His saying: ﴿By time, indeed mankind is in loss, except those who have believed and done righteous deeds and advised each other to truth and advised each other to patience﴾ [al-'Aṣr: 1–3]. So mutual advice to truth and patience is the perfection of worship after tawḥīd. And al-Fātiḥah in its entirety breathes the spirit of worship into the one who contemplates it, and the spirit of worship is the saturation of hearts with the fear of Allah, His awe, and hope in His bounty – not the known actions of deed or restraint or movements of the tongue and limbs. Worship is mentioned in al-Fātiḥah before the mention of prayer and its rulings, and fasting and its days. This spirit was present in the Muslims before they were obligated with these physical acts, and before the revelation of their rulings which were elaborated in the Qur'an to some degree. The movements and actions are only means by which one reaches the reality of worship, and the essence (mukh) of worship is reflection and taking lessons.

"As for reports and narratives: in His saying: ﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ is an explicit statement that there were peoples before who had passed on, and Allah had legislated laws for their guidance, and a crier cries out: Look well at the general affairs in which they were, and take lessons from them, just as He said to His Prophet, urging him to follow those prophets who came before him: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance﴾ [al-An'ām: 90]. There He clarified that narratives are only for admonition and lessons. And in His saying: ﴿Not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray﴾ is an explicit statement that apart from those upon whom favour was bestowed there are two groups: a group that went astray from the path of Allah, and a group that denied Him and opposed whoever called to Him; so the latter were surrounded by the divine anger and disgrace in this worldly life. The rest of the Qur'an elaborates for us, in the reports of nations, this summary in a manner that conveys the lesson, explaining the condition of the wrongdoers who opposed the truth, and the condition of those who adhered to it and endured what befell them in its cause.

So it becomes clear from the totality of what has preceded that al-Fātiḥah contains in summary the principles which the Qur'an elaborates in detail. Thus its being revealed first was in accordance with the sunnah of Allah (Exalted is He) in originating things, and on this basis al-Fātiḥah is worthy of being called "Umm al-Kitāb" (the Mother of the Book).

**The third:** Among the reports that are authentically established concerning its virtue is what al-Bukhārī narrated in his Ṣaḥīḥ from Abū Sa'īd ibn al-Mu'allā (may Allah be pleased with him), who said:

"I was praying in the mosque when the Prophet (ﷺ) called me, but I did not answer him. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I was praying.' He said: 'Did not Allah say: ﴿Respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you﴾ [al-Anfāl: 24]?' Then he said to me: 'Shall I teach you a sūrah that is the greatest of the sūrahs in the Qur'an before you leave the mosque?' Then he took my hand, and when we wanted to leave, I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, did you not say: "I will teach you a sūrah that is the greatest sūrah in the Qur'an"?' He said: '"All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds," it is the seven oft-repeated (al-sab' al-mathānī) and the great Qur'an which I have been given.'"

Aḥmad and al-Tirmidhī also narrated with a ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ chain from Abū Hurayrah something similar, except that the story is with Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and at its end: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, nothing like it has been revealed in the Torah, nor in the Gospel, nor in the Psalms, nor in the Furqān. It is the seven oft-repeated."

This ḥadīth and similar ones have been cited as evidence for the superiority of some verses and sūrahs over others, as is related from many scholars, among them Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh, Abū Bakr ibn al-'Arabī, and Ibn al-Ḥaḍḍār of the Mālikīs. And that is clear and evident.

Al-Bukhari narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "We were on a journey of ours, and we stopped. A slave-girl came and said: 'The chief of the tribe has been stung (by a scorpion or snake), and our men are absent. Is there anyone among you who can perform ruqyah (spiritual incantation)?' A man got up with her, and we did not think he had any knowledge of ruqyah. He recited over him and he recovered, so he was ordered to be given thirty sheep, and he gave us milk to drink. When he returned, we said to him: 'Did you know ruqyah well, or were you performing ruqyah?' He said: 'No, I only performed ruqyah with Umm al-Kitab (al-Fatihah).' We said: 'Do not do anything until we come to the Prophet ﷺ or ask him.' When we reached Madinah, we mentioned it to the Prophet ﷺ, and he said: 'How did he know it was a ruqyah? Divide (the sheep) and set aside a share for me.'"

Muslim and Abu Dawud narrated this in the same way. In some narrations of Muslim, it is stated that Abu Sa'id al-Khudri himself was the one who performed the ruqyah on that sallim, meaning the one bitten (they called him sallim as a good omen).

Muslim and al-Nasa'i narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said:

"While Jibril was sitting with the Prophet ﷺ, he heard a creaking sound from above him. He raised his head and said: 'This is a gate of the heaven that has been opened today; it has never been opened except today.' Then an angel descended from it, and he said: 'This is an angel who has descended to the earth; he has never descended except today.' He greeted and said: 'Rejoice in two lights that have been given to you, which no prophet before you has been given: the Opening of the Book (al-Fatihah) and the final verses of al-Baqarah. You will not recite a letter from them except that it will be given to you.'"

Muslim narrated from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Whoever prays a prayer in which he does not recite Umm al-Qur'an (al-Fatihah), it is deficient (khidaj), three times, not complete." It was said to Abu Hurayrah: "We are sometimes behind the imam." He said: "Recite it to yourself, for I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say:

'Allah, the Exalted, said: I have divided the prayer between Me and My servant into two halves, and for My servant is what he asks. When the servant says: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, Allah says: My servant has praised Me. When he says: ﴿The Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾, Allah says: My servant has extolled Me. When he says: ﴿Sovereign of the Day of Recompense﴾, Allah says: My servant has glorified Me - and at another time He said: My servant has entrusted (his affair) to Me. When he says: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾, He says: This is between Me and My servant, and for My servant is what he asks. When he says: ﴿Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor, not of those who have evoked (Your) anger or of those who are astray﴾, He says: This is for My servant, and for My servant is what he asks.'"

This much of the explanation of al-Fatihah is sufficient, and Allah speaks the truth and He guides to the right way.
